doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Quiet Pride, inspired by Elizabeth Catlett
summary: His commissioned suite inspired by Elizabeth Catlett's sculptures and plans to bring jazz, art and studies departments together.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: We’re going to be running out of tape soon. [To Rufus’ wife] Do you have any things that I should ask him?

Well I do want to talk about, you weren’t here, because I had my, it’s actually one of my most ambitious things, the Quiet Pride, which is the music that I was commissioned to write, inspired by Elizabeth Catlett’s sculptures. And that’s going to come out officially hopefully in September of this year. And it’s already been recorded and we’re developing a game plan and a booklet. There are five movements and I have five wonderful photos of her stuff. Very exciting for me. And I got a chance to at least teach the public a little bit with a group here that went very well on Wednesday. So this is part of my compositional stuff that is starting to take hold.
It’s a challenge to, you almost have two abstract things if you’re trying to portray a quality in a person, which is sort of abstract, and you have music which is sort of abstract.

Well it’s very interesting that people are saying, “Yeah it’s great that art is kind of inspiring other art.” And that has really become kind of neat, because my whole premise now is to go into the universities and have the jazz department, the art department, and the story of Elizabeth Catlett is pretty incredible if you come to really research and dig it. So we can go and have the Women’s Studies, or Afro-American Studies, and we have © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

these three different disciplines kind of interacting with one another, which is unheard of sometimes. There is very little of that — going into the schools, rehearse with the band, and have the art department bring some clay and some easels and sketch, while we rehearse. Just because it’s there. And then go into the sociology class and talk about her strifes and things that she had to deal with politically and racially in this country, and she still survived all that stuff you know. I mean it’s a story in itself. I didn’t know it was going to be like this, it’s got a life of its own now. But I’m happy to say that my recording is close to where I put her art in my mind in terms of the quality of her stuff.
Well best of luck with that.
It sounds like a natural for Hamilton College.
Sounds good to me. We’ll keep you in touch with that.
